note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Card, fact: The card defines marine simply as 'salt water' and says salt lakes such as Lake Torrens 'are not freshwater'. With only two groups, this implies inland salt lakes are marine biomes, which is false. Marine means seas and oceans; inland salt lakes are inland (non-marine) waters. The card should say salt lakes are salty inland waters, not marine, or avoid implying they fit the marine group.
- Question b, other: The clue 'Look at the salt in the water, not the size' rules out every option except the one that gives salt as the reason, so a student can answer from the clue without knowing the idea.

a.q: Which of these is a freshwater biome?
opts: A river
A coral reef
An ocean
A salt lake

a.clue: Freshwater means water with very little salt.

b.q: Tarni studies a large lake in Tasmania with water that has very little salt. How should she classify its biome?
opts: Freshwater, because its water has little salt
Marine, because it is a large body of water
Marine, because it is deeper than a river
Freshwater, because it is smaller than an ocean
b.why: Aquatic biomes are sorted by the salt in the water. This lake has little salt, so it is freshwater. Being smaller than an ocean is not the reason, because size is not the test.
b.clue: Look at the salt in the water, not the size.

problems.detail: The card says flatly that lakes and wetlands are freshwater biomes. Many Australian lakes are salt lakes, such as Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre and Lake Torrens in South Australia, and many wetlands are saline, such as mangroves and salt marshes. The card's own salt test would class these as not freshwater, so the wording could mislead. Say 'most lakes and many wetlands' or note that salt lakes exist.

version.title: Water biomes
card: Aquatic biomes are the biomes found in water. They are sorted into two groups: marine and freshwater.
Marine
the salty water of the seas and oceans. The open ocean and coral reefs are marine biomes.
Freshwater
inland water with very little salt. Rivers, most lakes and many wetlands are freshwater biomes.
Size and depth do not decide the group. A huge, deep lake with little salt is still freshwater, and a shallow coral reef is still marine.
version.remember: Marine biomes belong to the seas and oceans. Freshwater biomes are inland waters with little salt.

a.q: Which pair lists two marine biomes?
opts: An ocean and a coral reef
A river and a coral reef
A lake and the open ocean
A river and a wetland
a.why: Oceans and coral reefs are both part of the sea, so both are marine. A river or a lake is inland water, so a pair with one of them in it is not two marine biomes.
a.clue: Check both places in each pair.

b.q: Ravi visits a wide, deep lake in Tasmania. Its water is fresh, with very little salt. Which aquatic biome is it part of?
opts: Freshwater, as it is inland with little salt
Marine, as it is wide and deep like a sea
Marine, as large lakes count as marine biomes
Freshwater, as it is far smaller than an ocean
b.why: The lake is inland and its water has very little salt, so it is freshwater. Being smaller than an ocean is not the reason: size does not decide the group, and a huge lake can still be freshwater.
b.clue: Is this lake part of the sea?

a.best: An ocean and a coral reef

b.best: Freshwater, as it is inland with little salt

problems.detail: The stem says "Its water is fresh", which tells the student the group (freshwater) before they think about it, so the two marine options can be ruled out from the word alone. Saying only that the water has very little salt would make the student apply the card's rule.

check.summary: The facts and both answers are right. One small wording issue: question b's stem calls the lake's water "fresh", which half gives the answer away.
